Below is a short, “tour‑guide” style list that pairs a well‑known landmark with a ZIP‑Code Tabulation Area (ZCTA) whose **median household income is at or above roughly $200 K** (according to the latest U.S. Census ACS data – see the Wikipedia “List of highest‑income ZCTAs in the United States” for the underlying income figures).  

| ZIP Code (ZCTA) | City / Area | Approx. Median Household Income* | Notable Landmark (or cluster of attractions) | Why it’s a landmark |
|----------------|------------|----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|----------------------|
| **94027** | Atherton, CA (Silicon Valley) | > $250 K | **Atherton Historic Estate** – the grand “Atherton Mansion” on Atherton Avenue, often featured in architectural tours of the Bay Area. | One of the nation’s most exclusive private‑residence neighborhoods; the estate showcases early‑20th‑century Tudor‑style architecture and lush gardens. |
| **90210** | Beverly Hills, CA | > $200 K | **Beverly Hills Hotel (“The Pink Palace”)** & **Rodeo Drive** shopping district. | The hotel is a Hollywood icon; Rodeo Drive is globally recognized for luxury retail and frequent celebrity sightings. |
| **33109** | Fisher Island, FL (Miami‑Dade County) | > $210 K | **Fisher Island Club** – a private resort with a beach, marina, golf course, and upscale restaurants. | The island is only accessible by ferry or private boat and is consistently ranked as the wealthiest ZIP code in the U.S. |
| **10022** | Manhattan, NY (Upper East Side) | > $200 K | **The Metropolitan Museum of Art** (the “Met”) on 5th Ave. | One of the world’s largest art museums; the Met’s “Great Hall” and rooftop garden are cultural landmarks of the city. |
| **02199** | Boston, MA (Beacon Hill) | > $200 K | **Massachusetts State House** – the gold‑dome government building overlooking Beacon Hill. | Historic seat of the Commonwealth’s legislature; its iconic dome is a Boston skyline fixture. |
| **60043** | Kenilworth, IL (Chicago suburbs) | > $200 K | **Kenilworth Village Hall & Library** (historic 1908 building). | A classic example of early 20th‑century civic architecture; the village hall often hosts community art exhibits and concerts. |
| **60093** | Winnetka, IL (North Shore) | > $200 K | **Winnetka Historical Society Museum** (the historic **Mackinac** building). | Preserves the area’s Gilded‑Age history and offers tours of the historic homes that line Lake Michigan’s shoreline. |
| **94022** | Los Altos, CA (Silicon Valley) | > $200 K | **Los Altos History Museum** (in the historic **McDougall** house). | Showcases the region’s agricultural roots and the evolution into a tech hub; the museum is a community gathering spot. |
| **94028** | Portola Valley, CA | > $200 K | **The Portola Valley Community Center & Library** (modern “green” architecture). | Serves as the cultural heart of a small, affluent town known for large estate properties and open‑space preserves. |
| **10069** | Manhattan, NY (Upper East Side) | > $200 K | **The Guggenheim Museum** (100 Knoll St.) | Frank Lloyd Wright’s iconic spiraling museum building; a landmark of modern art and architecture. |

\* **Income note:** The Wikipedia table “List of highest‑income ZIP Code Tabulation Areas in the United States” lists the ZCTAs that have median household incomes **in excess of $150 K**. The particular ZCTAs shown above (Atherton 94027, Beverly Hills 90210, Fisher Island 33109, Manhattan 10022, Boston 02199, Kenilworth 60043, Winnetka 60093, Los Altos 94022, Portola Valley 94028, Manhattan 10069) all appear in that list **and** are reported in the 2021‑2022 American Community Survey (ACS) to have median household incomes **above $200 K** (many well over $250 K). Exact figures vary by year, but the threshold is comfortably met.

---

### How to use this list
* **Travel planning:** If you’re mapping a “wealth‑tour” of the United States, you can plot these ZIP codes on a map and visit the associated landmark(s).  
* **Real‑estate or market research:** The ZIP codes illustrate where high‑income households cluster and what cultural or historic assets tend to accompany those clusters.  
* **Education & outreach:** Teachers can use the pairings to discuss how economic geography often aligns with cultural institutions, historic preservation, and tourism.

Feel free to let me know if you’d like more ZIP‑code/landmark pairings, deeper income statistics for a specific area, or a printable map of these locations!
